not-on-my-street.title: Not on My Street
not-on-my-street.tagline: National news doesn't live on your street. Check it.

cards.headline: Home prices are crashing.
cards.question: In October, what happened to the typical home price in the DC metro compared with a year earlier?
cards.line: Typical DC metro price, down {{dc_price_change}} from a year earlier. Baltimore metro: {{balt_median_price}}, no change.
cards.explain: That's a dip, not a crash. Typical here means the median: half of homes sold for more, half for less.
cards.read: Prices are getting softer at the edges. Bright MLS does not expect big price drops in most markets over the next few months.

cards.headline: Nobody is buying homes.
cards.question: How did new purchase contracts in the DC metro change in October compared with a year earlier?
cards.line: New DC metro contracts in October. Showings fell {{dc_showings_change}}. Across the whole Bright MLS region, {{region_closed_sales}} homes still closed, {{region_closed_change}} fewer than a year earlier.
cards.explain: Fewer buyers is not zero buyers. Homes still sell. Each sale just takes more work.

cards.headline: Mortgage rates are finally dropping.
cards.question: On November 5, how did the average 30-year mortgage rate compare with a year earlier?
cards.line: Average 30-year rate on November 5. A year earlier it was {{rate_year_ago}}.
cards.explain: The headline is half right. Rates have eased for three weeks in a row, but they're still about a point above last year. Your buyers in DC and Maryland pay close to this national average.
cards.math: On a {{dc_median_price}} home with 20% down, that one point adds about {{payment_gap}} a month to principal and interest.

cards.headline: Unemployment is low. Jobs are fine.
cards.question: Which part of our area has unemployment higher than the national rate?

choices.text: DC, Prince George's and Charles counties

cards.line: Unemployment in DC, Prince George's and Charles counties in July. The whole Washington region, Northern Virginia included: {{wash_metro_unemp}} in September. The U.S.: {{us_unemp_sep}} in September.
cards.explain: Where you draw the map changes the story. The region as a whole looks fine. Its inner core is doing worse than the country.
cards.caution: The 5.2% is not seasonally adjusted and comes from a different month, so treat the comparison as rough.

cards.headline: Homes are sitting on the market for months.
cards.question: How long did a typical DC metro home take to sell in October?
cards.line: Typical time to sell in the DC metro, one day slower than a year earlier. Baltimore metro: {{balt_dom}} days, four days slower. Homes for sale across the region: up {{region_listings_change}}.
cards.explain: Typical homes still move in a few weeks. Buyers have more homes to choose from, so the first two or three weeks matter most.
cards.read: The homes that sit for months are usually priced too high for this market.

cards.headline: Home sales are moving onto the blockchain.
cards.question: What has Maryland done about putting property records on a blockchain?
cards.line: Gov. Moore signed SB 168 on May 26, 2026. The state assessments office has to report on using blockchain for property and lease records by {{md_study_due}}.
cards.explain: Deeds are still recorded by each county the usual way. A study is not a switch.
cards.read: Changes at Maryland closings are likely years away.

cards.headline: Crypto finally has clear rules.
cards.question: What happened to the CLARITY Act, the big crypto rulebook, in the Senate?
cards.line: The Senate vote on September 15, 2026. It needed 60 yes votes to move forward. The House passed the bill earlier.
cards.explain: Who polices most crypto is still unsettled. If a buyer wants to use crypto at a DC or Maryland closing, bring in a lender who handles it, early.

takeaways: National headlines don't live on your street. Check the local number before you react.
DC metro prices dipped a little. Contracts and showings fell a lot. Slower, not crashed.
Rates eased from the fall peak but are still about a point above last year.
Where you draw the map changes the jobs story.
Maryland is studying blockchain records, and the big crypto rulebook stalled. Nothing changes at closings yet.

wire-or-wait.title: Wire or Wait
wire-or-wait.tagline: Before any money moves, call a number you already have.
wire-or-wait.scenario: You're buying a $400,000 home in Prince George's County. You've put $8,000 down as earnest money, and you'll bring $41,850 to closing. These are example numbers.
wire-or-wait.setup: At your first meeting, Larkspur Title hands you a card: "We will never change wiring instructions by email. Call us at (301) 555-0142 before you send money." Your agent, Dana, gives you her cell. You save both.

messages.body: Inspection is Tuesday at 10. I'll meet you at the house.
messages.explain: This came from a number you saved, and it doesn't ask for money or private details. Replying is fine. Not every message is a scam.

messages.subject: URGENT: Updated wiring instructions
messages.body: Our bank is under a routine audit. Please send your $8,000 earnest money deposit to the new account below today so your closing is not delayed. Questions? Call us at (301) 555-0199.

choices.text: Reply to the email and ask

messages.explain: A change in wiring instructions is a stop sign, every time. Replying to the email only reaches the scammer.
flags: The address has a dash: larkspur-title.com, not larkspurtitle.com.
"Urgent" and "today" are there to rush you.
The bank "changed." Your title company told you it never changes wiring instructions by email.
The phone number in the email is not the one you saved.

messages.body: "Hey, it's Dana. Title switched banks, so I'm texting you the new account. Wire it tonight so we stay on schedule, okay?" The voice sounds just like Dana.

choices.text: Wire it tonight. It's Dana's voice
Text the number back to ask

messages.explain: AI can copy a voice from a short clip, like a video posted online. A familiar voice is not proof. Call the number you saved for Dana.
flags: It came from a number you don't know.
Same story as the email: the bank "switched."
Agents almost never handle wiring instructions. Title companies do.

messages.subject: Your Closing Disclosure is ready
messages.body: Your Closing Disclosure is ready to review. Tap here to log in to your secure portal.

choices.text: Tap the link in the email
Open the portal from the bookmark you saved at the start

messages.explain: This one looks right, and you do need to read your Closing Disclosure. Going in through your own bookmark means a fake link can never fool you, so it's the habit to build.
flags: The address matches your title company, but links can still be swapped. Your bookmark can't.

messages.subject: Final wiring instructions for closing
messages.body: Attached are your final wiring instructions for closing funds of $41,850. The account matches the one on the card we gave you at your first meeting.

choices.text: Wire it. It's from the right address
Call (301) 555-0142 and read the account back to them
Wire it, then call to make sure

messages.explain: Scammers break into the right email accounts too, then send messages that look exactly right. That's why the rule is about the number you call, not the address you see. Confirm first. A wire usually can't be undone.
flags: Nothing looks wrong. That's the point. You can't tell a hacked email by looking.

messages.body: "Hi, this is Morgan at Larkspur. Before we release your keys, please read me your bank account and routing numbers so we can confirm the transfer."

choices.text: Read the numbers. Caller ID matches
Give just the last four digits

messages.explain: Caller ID can be faked. The FCC calls it spoofing. If they called you, hang up and call the number you saved. Calling out is safe. Being called is not proof.
flags: They called you and asked for account numbers.
"Before we release your keys" is pressure at the worst moment.

messages.subject: You have a refund of $1,214
messages.body: Good news! You overpaid at closing. Reply with your bank account and routing numbers and we'll send your $1,214 refund this week.

choices.note: Your account numbers are now in a scammer's hands.

choices.text: Call (301) 555-0142 and ask if there's a refund

messages.explain: Scams don't stop at closing. Good news is bait too. Never send account numbers by email.
flags: The address adds "-escrow" to the name.
It asks for account numbers by email.

messages.body: Congrats again, neighbor! If you have a minute, here's where to leave me a review. No pressure.
messages.explain: It came from a number you saved and it asks for nothing private. Staying safe doesn't mean treating everyone as a scammer.

wire-or-wait.disclaimer_names: Every company, person, address and phone number in this game is made up.

ranks.name: Vault door
ranks.line: You stopped every scam and still answered the friendly texts.

ranks.name: Careful closer
ranks.line: You caught most of them. Look back at the ones that slipped.

ranks.name: Easy target, for now
ranks.line: That's what this game is for. Play again with the rule in mind.

takeaways: Before any money moves, call a number you already have. Never the one in the message.
A change in wiring instructions is a stop sign, every time.
The right email address, the right caller ID and a familiar voice can all be faked.
Never send account numbers by email or text, or read them to someone who called you.
If money goes to the wrong place, call your bank right away to recall the wire, then report it at ic3.gov. In 2025 the FBI's recovery team froze {{rat_rate}} of the money in cases reported to it.
wire-or-wait.loss_line: One slip sent money to scammers. With wire fraud, one slip is all it takes, so the habit has to hold every time.
